content.text:
DBB.Score gets the detailed statistics from a GraphQL API run by the app's maker NBN23, not from the DBB, and it uses the DBB's own game ids. I captured the traffic while opening one finished game (TSV Reinbek 2 – BSG Kisdorf Kaltenkirchen, 48:46).

## How the app gets its data

**Server:** `POST https://internal.nbn23.app/graphql`, with one GraphQL operation per screen. Other traffic:
- Team logos come straight from `basketball-bund.net/media/team/{id}/logo`.
- Player photos come from `storage.googleapis.com/nbn23-avatars/`.
- Braze (push and in-app messages) and Google's consent service also show up; neither carries statistics.

**Sign-in and Gold:**
- The app signs you in with Google through Firebase Auth (Firebase project `nbn23-competition-manager`) and sends the token as `Authorization: Bearer …`.
- Gold is a field inside that token: `"com.nbn23.germanapp": { "premium": true }`. The server sets it after the app sends your Play receipt with `mutation NewSubscription` (product `german_premium_yearly`).
- The app also sends `x-user-premium: true`. I didn't test whether the server checks the token, the header or both.
- Other headers: `x-package-name: com.nbn23.germanapp`, `x-package-version: 2.14.0`, `x-device-id`.

**Ids:** `matchFid` is the DBB's Spiel id (2843220 here), and the competition `fid` is the DBB's Liga id (54380). `projectKey` names the region (`dbbSH`). Competitions have a `freeContent` flag, which is `false` for this one, so it presumably marks free versus Gold content.

**Operations captured:**

| Operation | What it returns |
|---|---|
| `Match` (full) | Game header: Halle with Google place id, scores per quarter, both Kader with player ids and photos, coaches, status, game settings, AI pre- and post-match texts with audio |
| `Match` (with `actions`) | **Play-by-play**: every action with player, team, `code`/`subCode` (`POINTS`/`FREE_THROW`, `IN_ARC`, `FOUL`, `RECEIVE_FOUL` …), whether it scored, period, game clock in ms, court position |
| `MatchBoxscore(periods: [Int!])` | **Box score** per player and team: minutes, points, 2P/3P/FT made and missed, offensive/defensive rebounds, assists, turnovers, steals, blocks, fouls, FIBA efficiency, +/-. `periods: []` means the whole game; the P1–P4 buttons pass single quarters |
| `GetHomeData`, `GetUserFollows`, `GetSeasons`, `GetCompetition`, `CompetitionGroup`, `GetUserInfo`, `CreateUser` | Home feed, followed teams, Ligen and tables, account |

## Compared with the DBB's API that Korbjäger uses

For this same game, `basketball-bund.net/rest/match/id/2843220/boxscore` returns `statisticType: 1`, every player with zeros and an anonymised name, and `hasPlayByPlay: false`. So the detailed numbers don't come from the DBB's public data. NBN23 holds them itself, probably from its own digital scoresheet. That would mean Korbjäger can't get these statistics from the DBB at all, only from NBN23.

## Current state and caveats

- **Emulator:**
  - `dbbscore` is still running, rooted, with the proxy on (`10.0.2.2:8080`).
  - mitmweb is still recording.
  - After a reboot, the certificate has to be set up again with `/data/local/tmp/inject-ca.sh`.

It contains your valid token (it runs out after about an hour), your Play receipt, and real children's names and photo links. Under ADR 0019 none of it may go into the repo.
- **Terms of use:** the API is internal and undocumented. Using it in Korbjäger would almost certainly need NBN23's permission, beyond the open question of asking the DBB.

D="C:/Users/Wolfr/AppData/Local/Temp/claude/13fd550454c90f86/62506fb4-41aa-406c-990f-fad36afa0930/scratchpad/nbn23"; which jq; cat > "$D/nbn23.sh" <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Usage: nbn23.sh <Operation> '<variables JSON>'
#   nbn23.sh MatchBoxscore '{"matchFid":"2843220","projectKey":"dbbSH","periods":[]}'
set -euo pipefail
DIR="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")" && pwd)"
source "$DIR/secrets.env"
OP="$1"; VARS="${2:-{\}}"
QUERY_FILE="$DIR/$OP.graphql"
[ -f "$QUERY_FILE" ] || { echo "no query $QUERY_FILE" >&2; exit 1; }
GQL_OP="${OP%Actions}"   # MatchActions is the operation "Match" with the actions field

# 1. Refresh token -> Firebase ID token (valid 1 h), cached in .idtoken
TOKEN_FILE="$DIR/.idtoken"
if [ ! -s "$TOKEN_FILE" ] || [ $(( $(date +%s) - $(date -r "$TOKEN_FILE" +%s) )) -gt 3300 ]; then
  curl -sS "https://securetoken.googleapis.com/v1/token?key=$NBN23_API_KEY" \
    -H 'Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded' \
    --data-urlencode grant_type=refresh_token \
    --data-urlencode "refresh_token=$NBN23_REFRESH_TOKEN" \
  | jq -er .id_token > "$TOKEN_FILE"
  chmod 600 "$TOKEN_FILE"
fi

# 2. GraphQL request, headers as the app sends them
jq -n --arg op "$GQL_OP" --rawfile q "$QUERY_FILE" --argjson v "$VARS" \
   '{operationName:$op, query:$q, variables:$v}' \
| curl -sS --compressed https://internal.nbn23.app/graphql \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $(cat "$TOKEN_FILE")" \
    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    -H 'x-package-name: com.nbn23.germanapp' \
    -H 'x-package-version: 2.14.0' \
    -H 'x-user-premium: true' \
    -H 'user-agent: com.nbn23.germanapp' \
    --data-binary @-
EOF
chmod +x "$D/nbn23.sh"

No. DBB.Score is a **React Native** app with native screens; it doesn't wrap a website. I pulled the installed APK from the emulator and looked at what it contains:

- **React Native, new architecture:** `libreactnative.so`, `libjsi.so`, `libfbjni.so`, `libappmodules.so`, plus the generated modules for `react-native-screens`, `react-native-svg`, `safe-area-context`, the slider and the gesture handler. `libworklets.so` points to Reanimated or Worklets for animations.
- **Hermes:** the app code is `assets/index.android.bundle`, about 6.8 MB of compiled Hermes bytecode, not plain JavaScript.
- **Native modules:** Nitro Modules (`libNitroIap.so` handles the Play subscriptions), Fresco for images (`libimagepipeline.so`), Crashlytics.
- **A WebView is included:** `RNCWebView` appears in the code, so `react-native-webview` is bundled. It probably serves individual pieces, such as ads, the consent dialog or embedded content. The game screens themselves are native React Native views, and they get their data from the GraphQL API.
- **Play's integrity protection:** `libpairipcore.so` is Google Play's automatic integrity protection. It checks whether the app was installed from Play and wasn't modified. That's why patching the APK (option B earlier) would most likely have failed.

The JavaScript logic could be decompiled from the Hermes bundle with a tool like `hermes-dec`, including every GraphQL query, even ones we haven't captured yet. If you want that, say so.
